q: Which continent-wide scheme lets grid companies cancel out each other's opposite shortfalls and surpluses instead of ranking price offers?
answer: The imbalance netting platform: it has the netting function and the TSO-TSO settlement function and uses a multilateral TSO-TSO model, with no activation optimisation function and no common merit order lists (Article 22(2)).

q: Which of the continent-wide trading schemes has its blueprint drafted only by the grid operators that run the slowest back-up stage, rather than by all of them?
answer: The replacement-reserves platform: the proposal is developed by all TSOs performing the reserve replacement process under Part IV of Regulation 2017/1485 (Article 19(1)); for the other platforms it is all TSOs.

q: How long after the blueprint for the trading scheme covering back-up power that a dispatcher orders by hand is approved do grid companies have to get it running?
answer: Thirty months after approval of the implementation framework, or 12 months after approval of a modification proposal if one is submitted (Article 20(6)).

q: Eighteen months after sign-off on the trading scheme for back-up power released by computerised control, grid companies may suggest changes: what may those changes touch beyond how the scheme is rolled out?
answer: Also to the principles set in paragraph 2 of Article 21 (Article 21(5)); the equivalent paragraph for the manual-activation platform mentions only the framework (Article 20(5)).

q: Which exchange scheme has to be switched on only by operators that have at least one neighbouring operator running the same back-up stage?
answer: The replacement-reserves platform: TSOs performing the reserve replacement process that have at least one interconnected neighbouring TSO performing it (Article 19(5)).

q: How soon after sign-off must the scheme for offsetting opposite grid mismatches be running, and for which grid area must it at least be used?
answer: One year after approval of the implementation framework; at least for the Continental Europe synchronous area (Article 22(5)).

q: Under which approach to reserving border transmission room for back-up power are trades in electricity and offers of back-up power resolved in one single calculation?
answer: The co-optimised allocation process: capacity is allocated to energy bids and balancing capacity bids in a single optimisation process (Article 40(1)(b)).

q: What ceiling applies, relative to last year's available trading room across a border, when the reservation is justified by a study showing that it pays off?
answer: 5 % of the available capacity for energy exchange of the previous calendar year (10 % of installed technical capacity for new interconnectors) (Article 42(2)).

q: What fraction of last year's border trading room can be locked in for back-up power when the booking rests on comparing the worth on both sides and is made up to a week ahead?
answer: 10 % of the available capacity for energy exchange of the previous calendar year (or of installed technical capacity for new interconnectors) (Article 41(2)).

q: How is the worth of border room valued when grid companies merely pool their back-up power instead of buying it?
answer: Based on the avoided costs of procuring balancing capacity (Article 39(4)).

q: Which type of link between countries can have trading room booked for the very fastest stabilising power, contrary to the usual rule that only the safety buffer serves that purpose?
answer: Direct current (DC) interconnectors (Article 38(4)).

q: At a minimum, how often must grid companies recheck that room set aside through the pay-off-study route is still needed?
answer: At least every year (Article 38(8)).

q: Where can border room go if it was set aside for back-up power but the matching energy swap never used it?
answer: It is released for the exchange of balancing energy with shorter activation times or for operating the imbalance netting process (Article 38(9)).

q: What goal is stated for the arrangement whereby one operator can lean on a neighbouring region's capacity to bring the grid back to its normal rhythm?
answer: Enabling a TSO to perform the frequency restoration process by frequency restoration power interchange between LFC areas (Article 147(1)).

q: What goal is stated for the arrangement that cuts how much opposing correcting energy neighbouring regions deploy simultaneously?
answer: Reducing the amount of simultaneous counteracting FRR activations of the different participating LFC areas by imbalance netting power interchange (Article 146(1)).

q: What is the upper limit on how much counterbalancing power a region may swap when cancelling opposite corrections?
answer: It may not exceed the actual amount of FRR activation necessary to regulate the FRCE of that LFC area to zero without imbalance netting power interchange (Article 146(6)).

q: Who must be informed when a country lets a high-voltage grid company keep a power store despite the general ban?
answer: The decision to grant the derogation shall be notified to the Commission and ACER with the information about the request and the reasons (Article 54(3)); no such notification in Article 36.

q: Until which year must the decision to fund a new grid-side power store have been taken for a high-voltage grid company to keep the usual write-off period before phase-out?
answer: 2024 (Article 54(5)), where the battery is connected within two years, integrated, used only for reactive restoration of network security and not used to trade electricity.

q: Until which date must the decision to fund a new grid-side power store have been taken for a local-level grid company to keep the usual write-off period before phase-out?
answer: 4 July 2019 (Article 36(4)), subject to connection within two years, integration into the distribution system, use only for reactive restoration and no electricity trading.

q: Before approving an exception for a high-voltage grid company that wants to run a power store, what must the regulator have reviewed in advance regarding the open call for bidders?
answer: An ex ante review of the applicability of a tendering procedure, including its conditions (Article 54(2)(c)); Article 36(2)(c) speaks only of an assessment of the tendering procedure.

q: Which duty makes a local-level grid company purchase the power that offsets its own line losses in an even-handed, competitive way?
answer: Acting as a neutral market facilitator in procuring the energy it uses to cover energy losses, where it has such a function (Article 31(5)); a distribution system operator task, not listed in Article 40.

q: Which type of grid company has to take care of defence against hacking and of data handling among its listed duties?
answer: The transmission system operator: data management, including cybersecurity and data protection, is a listed responsibility (Article 40(1)(m)); the distribution operator list has no such item.

q: Which grid companies collect the money from scarce cross-border lines and handle payments for hosting the flows of neighbours' trade?
answer: Transmission system operators: collecting congestion rents and payments under the inter-TSO compensation mechanism (Article 40(1)(h)).

q: May a country oblige local grid companies to run green generators and combined heat-and-power plants first when scheduling plants?
answer: Yes: a Member State may require the DSO, when dispatching generating installations, to give priority to installations using renewable sources or high-efficiency cogeneration (Article 31(4)).

q: When may a local grid company skip competitive purchasing of grid-support products that have nothing to do with frequency?
answer: When the regulatory authority has assessed that market-based provision is economically not efficient and has granted a derogation; the obligation does not apply to fully integrated network components (Article 31(7)).

q: How long do grid companies have, counted from the decision to start, to submit a joint recommendation on redrawing price areas?
answer: Within 15 months of the decision to launch the review (Article 32(4)(b)(iii)).

q: How long do grid companies have, counted from approval of the assessment method, to submit a joint recommendation on redrawing price areas?
answer: No later than 12 months after approval of the methodology and assumptions (Article 14(6)).

q: When national energy regulators cannot agree on the approach for examining the layout of price areas, who takes the decision?
answer: ACER, within an additional three months, decides on the methodology, assumptions and alternative configurations (Article 14(5)).

q: As a last resort, who decides whether to redraw price areas if the countries involved cannot agree unanimously?
answer: The Commission, after consulting ACER (Article 14(8)).

q: Who must make public that a redrawing exercise for price zones has begun and what came out of it?
answer: ENTSO for Electricity, or the participating TSO if the review was launched by a single regulatory authority or TSO (Article 32(6)).

q: How often must the network operators' joint body present an overview of lasting bottlenecks inside and across price areas?
answer: Every three years (Article 14(2)).

q: For plants that start up from 2026, how small must a green plant be to remain excused from paying for the mismatches it causes?
answer: Below 200 kW (Article 5(4); 400 kW before 2026).

q: For plants that start up from 2026, how small must a renewable plant be to still get first call when the grid operator decides which plants run?
answer: Below 200 kW installed capacity (Article 12(5); 400 kW before 2026).

q: Which already-running subsidised plants, in service before mid-2019, may a country still excuse from paying for the imbalances they cause?
answer: Installations benefitting from support approved by the Commission under Union State aid rules and commissioned before 4 July 2019 (Article 5(2)(c)).

q: When does an older green plant that was scheduled ahead of others lose that benefit?
answer: From the date on which it becomes subject to significant modifications, at least where a new connection agreement is required or its generation capacity is modified (Article 12(6)).

q: If a multi-year border trading entitlement is cut because of an event beyond anyone's control, what does its owner get back?
answer: Compensation equal to the amount initially paid for the long-term transmission right in the forward allocation, from the TSO that invoked the force majeure (Article 56(3)).

q: When the grid is under acute threat and next-day border entitlements bought at auction get cut, how is the payout worked out?
answer: Equal to the price difference of the relevant markets between the bidding zones concerned (Article 72(3)(c)); the price paid is reimbursed if no zonal price is calculated in one of the zones (Article 72(3)(d)).

q: Who pays the owners of multi-year border entitlements that were cut for safe-running reasons before the next-day cut-off, and what is the sum based on?
answer: The concerned TSOs on the bidding zone border compensate the holders with the market spread (Article 53(2)).

q: Through which parties does the public notice about a sudden cut in booked border room reach traders?
answer: Through NEMOs (and directly to contractual parties holding explicitly allocated capacity) (Article 72(2)).

q: Inside what time window before delivery does the joint procedure for trimming multi-year border entitlements stop applying, and which process replaces it?
answer: For curtailments within 48 hours ahead of the start of the delivery day, the day-ahead and intraday capacity calculation process of Regulation 2015/1222 Article 29 applies instead (Article 25(1)).

q: Within what time must grid companies hand out their shares of the takings from scarce border room once the cash has arrived?
answer: As soon as reasonably practicable and no later than one week after the congestion income has been transferred (Article 73(3)).

q: Which two aims take precedence when deciding what to do with the takings from allocating border transmission room?
answer: Guaranteeing the actual availability of the allocated capacity including firmness compensation, or maintaining or increasing cross-zonal capacities (including network investments) (Article 19(2)).

q: By what calendar date each year must regulators brief the EU agency and publish a report on what was done with the takings?
answer: By 1 March each year (Article 19(5)).

q: Until what date may a country's regulators allow settlement intervals longer than a quarter of an hour?
answer: Derogations may be granted only until 31 December 2024 (Article 8(4)); from 1 January 2025 not exceeding 30 minutes where all regulators of the synchronous area granted an exemption.

q: How often must regulators in a region excused from the quarter-hour interval weigh costs against benefits of aligning it?
answer: At least every three years, in cooperation with the Agency (Article 53(3)).

q: Who tells the grid operator which volumes of back-up energy offers cannot be delivered after the cut-off for submitting offers?
answer: The balancing service provider reports unavailable volumes to the connecting TSO without undue delay, and to the DSO as well if it has a DSO connection point and the DSO requires it (Article 24(4)).

q: What must a proposal include if a grid company wants to pre-agree the price of delivered output in a deal for keeping resources on standby?
answer: A justification demonstrating higher economic efficiency; the exemption applies only to specific products and is proposed in the terms and conditions related to balancing (Article 16(6)).

q: Who may refuse an agreement to lend restoration capacity between operators, besides the one lending and the one borrowing, and on what ground?
answer: The affected TSO, as well as the providing or receiving TSO, may refuse when sharing would result in power flows that violate the operational security limits (Article 166(4)).

q: When borrowed restoration capacity turns out to be unavailable, who must cope with the resulting incidents?
answer: The control capability receiving TSO (Article 166(6)).

q: Who steers the power flow over a DC cable when restoration energy is traded between grids running at independent frequencies?
answer: The operator of each HVDC interconnector, following instructions from the reserve connecting TSO or the reserve receiving TSO (Article 176(4)).

q: How often must an exemption granted to some island grids from the automated restoration scheme be revisited?
answer: At least every 4 years (Article 145(2)).

q: How often must the bodies computing interconnection limits tell regulators about trimming applied when grid operators double-check the figures?
answer: Every three months, with location, amount and reasons (Article 26(5)).

q: What is the longest period for which the Commission may approve a scheme that pays power plants for being available?
answer: No longer than 10 years; capacity mechanisms are temporary (Article 21(8)).

q: Above what level of carbon output for each unit of electricity may newly started plants not be paid for standing ready?
answer: 550 g of CO2 of fossil fuel origin per kWh of electricity, for capacity that started commercial production on or after 4 July 2019 (Article 22(4)(a)).
